headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: Election Day: Here's what's at stake in the Bay Area as voters head to polls
headlines.description: Bay Area polls are open and voting is underway Tuesday for the November midterm election. California voters will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. From allocating funds aimed at boosting affordable housing to levying a tax on billionaires in the state, voters will also weigh in on 14 California propositions. Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2 There are also a host of key races in the Bay Area. The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Alameda County voters will choose between California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez for who will serve the Congressional District 14’s next full two-year term. Oakland residents will also have their say on whether Barbara Lee will continue to serve as mayor. In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. San Francisco voters are considering several propositions, including Prop B, which would pave the way for a public bank, and Prop G, which would reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Prop H if passed would establish a parcel tax to fund Muni. City voters will also weigh in on the Congressional District 11 race, where Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. In San Mateo County, Measure E in Redwood City would limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay would block proposed farmworker housing and Measure U aims to create an independent commission to draw supervisor districts in the county. In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. South Bay residents will also vote in mayoral races held in Milpitas, Morgan Hill and Santa Clara. Marin County County voters will decide on several measures related to paramedic and emergency medical services. City council seats are also up for election in Novato, San Rafael, Larkspur and Sausalito. In Solano County, voters will choose between Mike Silva and John Carli, who will face in a runoff for a supervisors district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E if passed by voters would establish a tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. Sonoma County voters will decide whether Mike McGuire or James Gallagher takes a seat redistricted by Proposition 50.

headlines.title: Trump and affordability loom over California governor's race between Becerra and Hilton
headlines.description: President Donald Trump, California’s notoriously high cost of living and political experience are on the ballot as voters decide Tuesday whether to elect Democrat Xavier Becerra or Republican Steve Hilton as the next governor of the nation’s most populous state. The winner will succeed Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who can’t seek a third term but is considering a White House run. Becerra, a former state attorney general, has promised to reaffirm California’s status as a liberal counterweight to the Trump administration’s Republican policies. Hilton, a former political adviser in the United Kingdom and Fox News host, has pitched himself as a fresh face ready to set the state back on track after 15 years of Democratic leadership. Hilton faces steep odds. Democrats make up roughly 45% of registered voters in California, compared to Republicans’ 25%. Mail voting has been underway for nearly a month. The Trump administration has sought to sow distrust in the state’s election system by alleging up to 20,000 noncitizens could be registered to vote. The Department of Justice has sued the state in an attempt to stop officials from counting any ballots cast by those people. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s demand on Monday after several lower courts also sided with California. State and local election officials say they follow federal law and the federal government’s numbers are likely inflated. Election experts say voting by noncitizens is rare and has not been shown to change the outcome of elections. Candidates argue over the value of experience Becerra, who also served in Congress and as U.S. health secretary in President Joe Biden’s administration, has argued that he’s best positioned for the job as someone with more than 35 years of experience in politics and government. Hilton has never held elected office. Becerra said at a CNN debate in September that the state needed a leader who could keep the “California dream” alive. “You can’t do it with someone who’s never served, who’s never balanced a budget the size of California, who’s never actually been there to defend people against the tyrant like Donald Trump,” he said. Meanwhile, Hilton has tried to turn his lack of political experience into an asset, arguing the more experienced Democrats who have been in charge have left Californians struggling to afford gas, housing and a college degree. “This is the most amazing state and the most amazing country on Earth, and it’s because we’ve got this rebel spirit,” he said at the debate. “That spirit is being crushed by this bloated, nanny-state bureaucratic government that Xavier has been a part of for 36 years.” A chaotic primary gave way to a low-key general election matchup The two candidates emerged from a large primary field with half a dozen prominent Democrats and two notable Republicans. Becerra wasn’t considered a top contender for the first months of his campaign. That changed when former Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell, who had been viewed as a front-runner, dropped out of the race and resigned from Congress following allegations he sexually assaulted several women. He’s denied the accusations. His departure caused the party establishment and voters to look for a more reliable alternative, and they found one in Becerra. Since then, Becerra has run a relatively low-key campaign, not holding nearly as many public events or press availabilities as Hilton. He’s sought to take advantage of Trump’s deep unpopularity in the state by tying Hilton to Trump, noting the president has endorsed the Republican. Becerra’s campaign launched a website that lists quotes of Hilton expressing support for the president and his policies. The site includes illustrations of the two Republicans standing side by side. Hilton, meanwhile, has tried to break through by releasing splashy ads, sometimes with AI-generated content, to encourage voters who typically choose Democrats to try something new. He’s also tried to appeal to the public by making ambitious promises, including pledging to abolish the DMV and cut gas prices to $3 a gallon, a rate the state hasn’t seen in years. His promise to bring change as a Republican candidate running in California has resonated with some voters. Richard Hartman, an independent voter living outside Sacramento who works in the construction industry, said he was leaning toward voting for Hilton to bring balance to the Democrat-dominated state. He’s particularly concerned about homelessness and the high cost of living. “Nothing works without balance,” he said. “You can’t stand on one leg and walk around. You have to have two feet, and I think that’s the same thing in politics.” Both candidates highlight their families’ immigrant stories For all their differences, Becerra and Hilton share at least one thing in common: Both come from immigrant backgrounds. Hilton’s parents fled communism in Hungary and settled in the United Kingdom, where Hilton was born. Hilton went on to advise former Prime Minister David Cameron before moving to California in 2012. If he wins, he would be the first immigrant to serve as governor since Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger left office in 2011. Becerra was born in Sacramento to a mother from Mexico and a father who was born in California and raised in Mexico. He’s made appealing to Latino voters a key part of his campaign strategy, including by releasing ads and social media posts in Spanish. He’d be the state’s first Latino governor since the late 19th century. His background has appealed to some Californians with Mexican heritage, including Joy Torrez, a Democratic retiree in Sacramento. She proudly planned to vote for him. “I’ve read about him, and I’m really pleased,” Torrez said.

headlines.title: California could become the first state to tax billionaires' wealth
headlines.description: California could become the first state in the nation to tax the net worth of billionaires Tuesday under a ballot measure that has divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history as the ultra-rich scramble to figure out whether they would pay the tax or flee. Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warns it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them. The “no” side has raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who have poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Billionaires are already bracing for its approval. Some of them, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state after the measure was unveiled. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company. Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, say it’s needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years. “It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions. But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition opposing it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents. Californians are divided on the measure. Likely voters were slightly more likely to oppose the measure than support it in a poll conducted in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California, with 52% saying they would vote “no” and 46% saying they would vote “yes.” That’s an apparent shift from a PPIC survey conducted in early September, when 52% of likely voters said they’d vote for the tax and 46% said they’d vote against it. Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it. “Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.” Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.” Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it, which are also on this year’s ballot, passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee has raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin. Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million. Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.” Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said. “We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.

headlines.title: Testimony slated to start in retrial of Sierra LaMar murder case
headlines.description: Testimony in the retrial of the man accused of killing Morgan Hill teenager Sierra LaMar is expected to start Tuesday. LaMar disappeared on her way to her bus stop before school in 2012. Five years later, Antolin Garcia-Torres was found guilty in her murder, but that decision was later overturned by an appellate court because the district attorney’s office introduced three unrelated kidnapping accusations against him. During opening statements Monday, the Santa Clara County prosecutor tried to paint a picture of the day LaMar disappeared in March 2012. He explained that even though LaMar has not been found, there is evidence connecting LaMar and Garcia-Torres. He said carpet fibers from Garcia-Torres’ car were found on LaMar’s clothing and her DNA and a strand of her hair her found in the trunk. “Sierra’s body has never been found, yet traces of Sierra were found in the car driven by that man right there,” prosecutor O’Bryan Kenney said, pointing at Garcia-Torres. “Traces of that man were found on Sierra‘s clothes. Traces of that man’s car were found on Sierra’s clothes.” Garcia-Torres’ attorney said it was all evidence that was mishandled. “You want to carefully handle the items so that you don’t cross-contaminate or contaminate these items because you’re mishandling the evidence,” defense attorney Al Lopez said. “There’s protocols for this, and you’re going to see they weren’t followed.” Lopez also told the jury that they would be hearing about someone else who could’ve been involved. The trial is expected to resume at 9 a.m. Tuesday and stretch into next year. Morgan Hill Nov 2 Morgan Hill Oct 2 Sierra LaMar murder case: Judge will not recuse himself, jury selection next week

headlines.title: 17-year-old arrested in connection with deadly shooting at Solano Town Center in Fairfield
headlines.description: Police have arrested a 17-year-old boy accused of a deadly shooting inside a Fairfield mall that left a pregnant woman dead and six other people wounded. Investigators said the teen was identified within hours after a school resource officer recognized him in surveillance footage from the store. Police body camera and SWAT video captured the suspect’s arrest outside a home in Suisun City. He now faces suspicion of murder and attempted murder charges stemming from Friday night’s shooting at the Solano Town Center. “After reviewing surveillance footage from the store, the school resource officer recognized the suspect as a former student and provided that information to the detectives,” said Michelle Belya, Fairfield Police Department public information officer. Authorities revealed that the teen had previously spent time in juvenile hall last year in connection with a shooting into a car in the parking lot of a local high school. Investigators said that on Friday night, he opened fire inside the Spirit Halloween store, targeting one customer but hitting seven people. “There was obviously some kind of disagreement prior to the situation,” said Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall. One of the victims, 31-year-old Constance Hages, was killed. Police confirmed she was pregnant, and the district attorney will decide whether the teen should face an additional murder charge in connection with the death of her unborn child. Six others were injured, including one person who remains in critical condition while others are stable. The grandmother of one teenage survivor, who was shot in the stomach, spoke anonymously about the tragedy. “You never think sending your child out to a Halloween store that they maybe won’t come back anymore. It’s just unreal,” she said. “You just didn’t ever think of how harmless it could’ve been, something you usually do, and then it turned into a literal nightmare.” Chief Marshall emphasized the urgent need to address youth violence and accountability. “How many more people need to get shot or killed before we start making some changes? We need to hold kids accountable,” Marshall said. Police believe the 17-year-old was the sole shooter, though the investigation remains ongoing to determine if anyone else was involved. Fairfield Oct 31 Fairfield Oct 30 1 dead, 6 hurt following shooting at Solano Town Center in Fairfield

headlines.title: Anthropic posts $17B quarterly revenue but losses continue in fresh IPO filing
headlines.description: Anthropic’s quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing released on Monday. The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude chatbot also disclosed that it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that’s due to be spent in the next 12 months. The numbers were released about a week after Anthropic issued its original IPO filing in preparation for what’s expected to be a blockbuster Wall Street debut later this month. The document, like the earlier filing, shows the company’s revenue is growing but — like its AI rivals — profit is still elusive. Anthropic’s revenue grew by 13 times to $33.2 billion for the first nine months of the year, but it reported a net loss of $104 billion, including a charge of $94 billion for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements. On a quarterly basis, Anthropic lost $23.3 billion on revenue of $17 billion. The filing gave no indication of how much the company ultimately expects to raise, or what the shares will be priced at when it goes public. Anthropic has previously said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

headlines.title: Students reportedly overdose at San Jose school Halloween party
headlines.description: A possible drug overdose during an afterschool party at a San Jose school has left many parents concerned and frightened. Multiple sources tell NBC Bay Area the incident occurred Thursday evening when two students had to be hospitalized after suffering an apparent drug overdose at a Sheppard Middle School Halloween party. One source familiar with the case said it was an over-the-counter drug the students took. The school district was not disclosing Monday what drug the teenagers are suspected of taking. District officials said they have launched an investigation. In an email to NBC Bay Area, the superintendent said the district is limited in the specific details it can share and are taking the matter seriously. The superintendent also said the district is working to determine any necessary follow-up actions. Both students involved are seventh graders at Sheppard Middle School. Both students are out of the hospital and recovering at home, according to the superintendent. “This absolutely concerning. We are talking about teens,” said Harsha Ramchandani, a chief medical officer at Bay Area Community Health. Ramchandani is not involved with the Sheppard Middle School teens, but said over-the-counter drugs can cause serious harm if not taken cautiously — drugs like Benadryl and cough medicine, including Tylenol. “That can cause hallucinations, dangerous heart rhythms, seizure, coma, even death,” she said. Ramchandani said an overdose occurs when the body is not able to handle the drugs a person ingests. The doctor said there was a 31% increase in child exposure to Benadryl, according to the CDC. An exposure is when a parent or a school official called the National Poison Control hotline to report a child has come in contact with the drug.

headlines.title: 1 dead in Sunnyvale apartment fire
headlines.description: One person died in a Sunnyvale apartment fire Sunday afternoon, and investigators are still working to determine what sparked the blaze. Fire crews were sent to 1235 Wildwood Ave. about 12:30 p.m. after receiving multiple calls about a fire in the building. When they got to the scene, crews found a unit fully engulfed in flames and were able to evacuate residents, including people in the four units impacted by the fire, Sunnyvale Department of Public Safety officials announced Monday. One person was found dead inside the unit where the fire started, officials said. The fire was under control within about 40 minutes and crews prevented it from spreading to other buildings. The cause of the fire and the circumstances surrounding the death are still under investigation. No additional details were provided.

headlines.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
headlines.description: The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots from people the federal government claims are noncitizens, a decision that came hours before the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections. The high court refused to immediately intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls. The swift rejection capped a string of losses for the president’s effort to intervene in the election before the counting of ballots to decide who controls Congress in the last two years of his second term. No justices publicly dissented. “The Court rejected Trump’s emergency request without even asking the other side to respond,” California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, posted on X. “Democracy won.” Several lower courts also rejected the Justice Department’s push to set aside the challenged California ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. And in a case that revolved around the future certification of Alaska’s election results, a judge did not even hold a hearing before dismissing a Trump-ordered suit to prevent a possible Democratic Senate win. The high court did not detail its reasoning in the California ballot case, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, also a Democrat, noted the administration’s legal losing streak in a statement. “Courts have now rejected the Trump Administration’s attempts to interfere in California’s elections not once, not twice, not three times, but four times — from the district court to the Ninth Circuit to the U.S. Supreme Court,” Bonta said. “This latest decision should put an end to the Administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders.” Voting by noncitizens is rare in the US The Republican administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite it being a rare problem. California officials said the administration’s list appeared to be filled with errors and said setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters. Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration’s efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution. “The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” Chief Judge James Boasberg wrote. Later Monday, ruling in a separate case, Boasberg declined to issue yet another order that the administration cease its demands. He ruled that Democratic groups that sued did not have legal standing and that the issue already had been dealt with by states and the courts. The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted. Its push has faced not only the remarkable series of losses in court, but criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable. During a hearing over whether to lift her order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, U.S. District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department’s data. “Would you agree there’s a high error rate?” the San Francisco-based judge asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney. “That’s a fair statement,” Kao said. “That’s why we ask for the registrars’ aid in verifying these are all valid voters.” At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department’s Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote. “This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list. Rather than lift her order, Thompson late Monday expanded it to require the Department of Justice to inform her ahead of time of any criminal investigations or prosecutions involving its noncitizen list. Californians have already been casting ballots for weeks Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. Each of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters is mailed a ballot, and more than 6 million have already been returned, according to Associated Press elections data. “The DOJ’s baseless challenge was yet another attempt at federal overreach and voter suppression,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, said in a statement in reaction to the Supreme Court decision. “We will not stand for the Trump Administration’s bullying campaign, and we will continue to use every tool at our disposal to ensure the American people’s voices are not silenced.” California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible. Lower courts swiftly sided with the state, with a district judge warning last week that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.” ___ Associated Press writers Sophie Austin in Sacramento, California, and Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed to this report. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court.
headlines.source: Lindsay Whitehurst | The Associated Press and Nicholas Riccardi | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Golden State Valkyries reflect on winning WNBA championship
headlines.description: Golden State Valkyries players took time Monday to reflect on capturing the franchise’s first WNBA title in just its second season of existence. Despite ongoing celebrations since winning it all Saturday night in San Francisco, most of the players said the gravity of capturing the WNBA crown still hasn’t soaked in just yet, except for Finals MVP Gabby Williams. “I was in bed by midnight after the game,” she said. “I just wanted to be with my friends and family. I mean, the game was early, so we did party. It’s been very calm. I’ve just had a moment to kind of soak it in. I didn’t have any expectations, but if I did, I thought it would just be party and whirlwind and energy. I found a very, I don’t know, just like serenity in everything that I’ve just loved.” Valkyries fans will have the chance to celebrate the team during Wednesday’s championship parade in San Francisco. “I’m expecting them to show up, show out,” center Kiah Stokes said. “I want it to be Halloween again, like come in the costumes. I just want it to be a big party. Just enjoy the moment. Let’s celebrate. Let’s have some fun. This is insane. I just want to feel the same energy that we have in ‘Ballhalla.’ I want to feel that at the parade.” Golden State Valkyries Nov 1 Golden State Valkyries 23 hours ago Golden State Valkyries Nov 1 ‘Closer' Gabby Williams validates Joe Lacob's hype in Valkyries' WNBA title win

headlines.title: 2 dead, 2 injured in shooting at Monterey County's Moss Landing
headlines.description: Two people were shot and killed at Moss Landing State Beach in Monterey County early Monday morning and two others were injured. The circumstances around the shooting were being investigated by the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office Monday, along with California State Parks police. Spokespeople for the agencies provided few details about the shooting in a press briefing Monday afternoon near the scene on Jetty Road, which leads to the beach. Jetty Road and Moss Landing State Beach were closed to the public on Monday. Monterey County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Commander Andres Rosas said the Sheriff’s Office was not yet ready to declare the deaths homicides and said there were several unknown elements to the case as of Monday afternoon, including a potential motive or identity of a suspect. Monterey County sheriff’s deputies, California Highway Patrol officers, and State Park rangers responded to a person’s report of hearing gunshots at about 2 a.m. The Sheriff’s Office had earlier said the shooting happened just after midnight. Two people were found dead at the scene with injuries that Rosas at first declined to describe. When pressed by reporters, he confirmed the two died from gunshot injuries. A third victim was found at the scene and was brought to the hospital with injuries that Rosas again declined to elaborate on, but characterized the injuries as not-life-threatening. A fourth victim arrived at the hospital on their own while the response was underway. Rosas said he was unsure about the nature of their injuries or their status as of Monday afternoon. Chief Ranger Mike Dippel said the beach closes at sundown, but a gate that would keep vehicles from entering the area is frequently left open because there are not enough staff to open it early in the morning. A nearby scene at the beach that appeared to have been a party was being investigated by the Sheriff’s Office, which is leading the case at the request of State Parks, but Rosas said it was unknown if the crime scene was connected to the site of the party. He said there was no active shooter in the area when law enforcement arrived, leading the Sheriff’s Office to declare there was no ongoing threat to the community. Assemblymember Dawn Addis, D-Morro Bay, who represents the area, said she was in contact with the Sheriff’s Office and thanked them for their response. “My heart is with those who are affected by this heinous violence,” Addis said in a statement. “We must continue to work to end gun violence, and I am committed to doing so.”
